structure.title: Act I – Act II, scene 1 · The soldiers return · Friends set about matchmaking
structure.text: Claudio wants to marry Hero. Beatrice and Benedick seem able to resume an old quarrel within seconds of meeting. Their friends decide that if direct courtship seems unlikely, each might be persuaded by a conversation overheard by accident.

structure.title: Act II, scene 2 – Act III · Two kinds of staged evidence
structure.text: The scheme for bringing the quarrelling pair together has a vicious counterpart. A man who believes he has seen for himself can be much harder to correct than one who knows he has only received a rumour.

structure.title: Acts IV–V · A wedding becomes an accusation
structure.text: A public ceremony gives an accuser an audience and leaves its intended bride very little chance to reply. Away from the leading men, an uncelebrated night watch has been listening to something that actually happened.

people.name: Beatrice and Benedick
people.text: Their remarks have the precision of people who know exactly where the blow will land. They are attractive company partly because either can change the other's mood. A serious disagreement will ask more of that intimacy than wit can manage.

people.name: Claudio and Hero
people.text: He declares himself through a prince's good offices. She lives among men who are remarkably willing to answer questions in her place. Courtship gives them fewer chances to know one another than their engagement suggests.

people.name: Dogberry
people.text: He takes pride in language that repeatedly gets away from him. People of higher rank can scarcely listen to him, a serious disadvantage for a town whose useful evidence has arrived at his level.

context.title: Honour needs an audience
context.text: Both a woman's reputation and a soldier's public standing depend upon other people's accounts of their conduct. A private suspicion can therefore become an occasion for a man to demonstrate his honour at a woman's expense.

notice.text: Look for a listener who thinks nobody sees him listening.
notice.why: People give particular credit to words apparently never meant for their ears. The play gets joy and cruelty alike out of the difference between a private conversation and a well-staged one.
Beatrice puts an abrupt demand to Benedick. Listen to what happens to the rhythms of their conversation when he must decide whether his gift for repartee amounts to a willingness to act.

opening: Beatrice and Benedick enjoy insulting each other so much that their friends suspect a little encouragement could turn the habit into love. Nearby, a younger couple needs almost no encouragement at all. Shakespeare lets overheard conversations and staged evidence work on both romances, producing delight in one place and serious injury in another. The pleasure of watching clever people fooled sits beside a harsher discovery: a woman's reputation can be destroyed very quickly when a man finds suspicion easier than asking her what happened.
